newsitem.title: USA: Clinton faces tough call on Mexico certification.
newsitem.headline: Clinton faces tough call on Mexico certification.

text.p: President Bill Clinton faces a tough decision this week on whether to certify Mexico as an ally against drug trafficking.
His administration must announce by Saturday the verdicts on Mexico and 31 other countries in the certification process.
Mexico has passed that annual test since 1986, when Congress mandated that the White House must examine whether major drug producing or transit countries cooperate with the United States.
But last week, Washington was caught by surprise when Mexico dismissed its top anti-narcotics official, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez, charging that he had ties to a drug kingpin.
"Until the arrest of the general, there was no question about Mexico's certification," said a White House official who requested anonymity. "Now we're assessing its case".
Besides being the United States' third largest trading partner, Mexico is also home to cartels that smuggle cocaine, heroin, methamphetamines and marijuana into U.S. territory.
Decertified countries face U.S. economic sanctions. Afghanistan, Burma, Colombia, Iran, Nigeria and Syria were blacklisted in 1996 and are expected to repeat that fate.
Yet a third possibility is a "vital national interests" certification, a waiver reserved for governments that fail to meet the standards for full recognition.
Under that cover, the United States can keep sending aid to a country and does not have to vote against its requests for loans from the World Bank and other multilateral lenders.
It also allows the U.S. government to continue offering export credits and investment guarantees, without which U.S. sales to Mexico could drop and widen the bilateral trade gap.
Clinton has yet to receive final recommendations on certification from Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who is due back on Tuesday from a tour to Europe and Asia.
Foreign Relations committee chairman Sen. Jesse Helms (R-NC) has long pushed for Mexico's decertification.
The ranking Democrat on his panel, Delaware Sen. Joseph Biden, on Monday urged Clinton to grant Mexico only a "vital national interests" certification.
Albright, in a Sunday interview with ABC news programme "This Week", acknowledged that a waiver was a possibility for Mexico, only to add that she did not want to prejudge.

Nevertheless, she and other U.S. officials praised Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo for removing the tainted general within days of certification, which was viewed in Washington as a sign of his commitment to fight corruption.

"The investigation and arrest of Gen. Gutierrez only underscored the problem and strengthens our determination to assist the government of Mexico," State Department spokesman Glyn Davies said on Monday.
In Mexico, Foreign Relations Secretary Angel Gurria told a radio interviewer on Monday that a negative evaluation from Washington would cause "a fracture in the bilateral relationship".
Clinton, a champion of strong links with Mexico, plans to travel there in April.

A full certification, however, could be questioned in the Republican-controlled Congress, especially since top U.S. officials lionised Gutierrez as an honest and no-nonsense commander weeks before he was accused of taking bribes.
The U.S. ambassador to Mexico praised the country's antinarcotics efforts on Monday and suggested Mexico would win the U.S. government's certification.

"I think there has been improvement in the fight against Mexican drug-traffickers," Ambassador James Jones told reporters in Mexico City after meeting leaders of the conservative opposition National Action Party.
"My government wants to collaborate with Mexico, the enemy are the drug-traffickers. It will take a lot of cooperation between our countries to succeed in that fight," he said.
